chapters.title: Deep Dive I: Two Ramps and a Lever
Deep Dive II: The Clockwork That Cannot Stop

lines.text: A small desktop: three windows, a dock, twelve photographs.
Drag a window. It glides, and settles.
Every move is worked out by one neural network, built with a library called Handwired. This window shows it, live.
Even the wallpaper maps it: one arc for each weight, each number it multiplies by. Nine thousand, nine hundred and nine.
Where did those weights come from?
Somebody trained it. A tool converted ordinary code. Or it isn’t really a network.
They hang on this copper line, as paper tags. We'll test every one.
And one more tag, blank for now: why would anyone build it this way?
A scrap of JavaScript a child could check. If a is more than four, ten. If not, twelve.
Build it from ramps, the stuff of neural networks. Five gives ten; three, twelve.
Give it four and a half.
Eleven. Neither ten nor twelve.
Nothing’s broken. It was built for whole numbers, and it took that on trust.
This film is about promises like that: who tied them on, who doubted them, and how long they held.
In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts tied on the oldest tag. Handwired never cites them.
The tag: a neuron is a logic gate. Neural events, they wrote, "can be treated by means of propositional logic."
Nothing in their nets learned. Someone chose every connection, by hand.
In 1951, at RAND, Stephen Kleene showed such a net is a finite machine.
He called the patterns it can recognise regular events.
Our reading: a finite net remembers only so much; anything unbounded comes from outside. Hang that on the line.

terms.gloss: the patterns a finite machine can recognise

lines.text: In 2020, one human neuron's branches answered either input but not both: a job thought to need layers of gates.
As biology, the logic-gate tag frayed. As engineering, it never came down.
In 2019, a younger tag: learn the weights, don’t write them.
Rich Sutton tied it on in The Bitter Lesson. Six days later, Rodney Brooks replied, "I think Sutton is wrong".
Some kept writing weights anyway, as proofs and test beds.
Eighty-three years after the oldest tag, someone has written a network’s weights by hand, to run a desktop.
The third of June, twenty twenty-six: Cheng Lou, Handwired's author, makes his first commit.
Four months and two renames later: Handwired.
Its tutorial: “A numeric program is a fixed list of operations over 32-bit floats”.
You don't write the list. Builder code, ordinary JavaScript run once, appends to it.
One guess falls at once, for the library itself. The docs: “No tool converts existing JavaScript source into a program.”
Every number the program reads or keeps is a cell in one table. A toggle has twenty.
A wire is a position: where a number lives.
Four instructions: a weighted sum, a gated product, a snap to a whole number, a read from a list.
Each step rounds to a thirty-two-bit float, a number that keeps about seven digits. Even whole numbers stay exact only to about seventeen million.
Somebody trained it? The desktop’s README: “Every weight of the program is written by builder code, and none is trained.”
That guess was ours.
And the Notes window? “The program holds no text.” Hang that on the line.
Back to four and a half. In JavaScript, only the chosen side runs.
A network has no if.
Bend a hinge: flat, then up. A ramp is all a ReLU is.
This one wakes at four. Three gives nought. Five gives one. A hundred gives ninety-six.
A second ramp wakes at five. Take it from the first.
Nought up to four, one from five: a bit. Whole numbers sit on the corners: the whole trick, and the whole caveat.
Two belts carry both answers, every time: ten and twelve. The bit opens one shutter, shuts the other.
Say the side you didn’t choose overflows, past the biggest float, to infinity. Nought times infinity isn’t nought. It isn’t a number at all.
Now four and a half. The bit reads a half: half of ten, half of twelve.
Eleven.
Every if here is a dimmer switch. The program’s job: keep it fully on, or fully off.
Past nearly seventeen million, floats skip whole numbers.
Just past it, the second ramp’s input rounds down. A bit meant for nought or one reads two. Answer: eight.
Another way to make a bit, in one instruction: add a huge odd number to a score, then take it away.
Up there floats sit one apart, so the score snaps whole. Ties go to the even side: a half snaps up, to one.
Each trick is exact. Against what? The thirty-two-bit calculation, not JavaScript’s usual sixty-four-bit doubles.
Fit columns in a window seventeen hundred and thirty-two pixels wide. Doubles fit seven; thirty-two-bit floats fall a hair short.
Why not doubles everywhere? A September study tried. Of twenty thousand percent labels, nearly nineteen thousand went wrong.
More precision broke it. Keep thirty-two-bit order at the rounding points alone, and every label came back.
The real library won’t compare until you promise a range.
Promise more, that a is a whole number, and the comparison takes two operations.
Now break the promise: four and a half, down a wire tagged whole.
Eleven again. A validator objects.
As the docs put it, “Declarations are promises from the caller, not proofs.”
Who tied it on? The caller. Who doubted it? The validator. How long it held? While the input stayed honest.
Promise only a range, and it must tell the tiniest difference from none. It magnifies by two to the hundred and forty-ninth.
The faintest difference becomes a full bar. A sixteen-operation comparison, and four and a half gives ten. Correct.
Sixteen against two. One honest sentence about your input saves fourteen operations.
Now feed the program's operations into a loom, a hundred and thirty layers deep.
Each step drops into the first layer after the steps it needs.
Copper threads add. Indigo threads subtract. Most of it is empty air.
The README calls it "a giant matmul": a matrix multiplication, the sums graphics cards are built for.
Sums of sums are still sums, so some fold together. But a gate is a bend: nothing merges across one.
The longest chain of gates runs seventy-one deep.
So it is a network, in the plain sense: weighted sums, with ReLU gates between.
That guess was ours too.
Step back. The wallpaper draws these same threads: one arc per weight.
And the Notes window? On the thirteenth of October its text moved to the browser, and the loom shed most of its threads.
The desktop runs as JavaScript on the main processor. On a graphics card, an older build ran fifteen to twenty-seven times slower, its steps one after another.
So what is a graphics card, a GPU, for? Hang that on the line.
In the docs' words: "The program runs every operation on every frame and can't stop early, so a loop becomes a count, a tree, a table, or the same work on every item."
The looping lives outside, in the host: the plain JavaScript around it.
Flick the toggle, and the event is queued with its time.
Inputs in. The loom runs once. Next state copied back. The page moves.
When nothing moves, the clock rests: between frames, never inside one.
The windows move on springs, and springs need time.
One step multiplies two numbers, the window's distance from home and its speed: at rest, it comes out moving.
Three hundred steps is that multiplication, squared and squared again. JavaScript works it out ahead, as four numbers; the program applies them in fourteen operations, for any count.
Past three hundred steps in one frame, stepping stops, and every window snaps home.
Replay one session at two frame rates, and the familiar loop drifts up to three hundred and fifty-nine pixels apart.
Handwired saves only at events and fixed checkpoints. Other frames replay from the last save, are drawn, and thrown away. In its tests, every frame rate then matches exactly.
One run per frame? That held until mid-September. Now a busy drag frame runs about seventeen.
A count. Which row is under the pointer? A loop stops at the first match. Here every row answers, and we count the yeses: three.
A tree. Running totals in a row: each waits for the last, seven steps deep. In pairs, then pairs of pairs: three or four.
In thirty-two-bit floats, grouping changes the final digit. The tree is slower here, but drifts far less.
A table. As arithmetic, you test all ten thousand rows, zero out all but one, and add: thirty thousand operations. Or one index read.
To sort, do the same work on every item: each card counts who comes before it. Nothing swaps.
Filtering too: each item counts its place, and a fixed rack takes the first three.
The desktop's Monitor window admits it: "Only 64 rows are drawn at a time."
Kleene's finite machine, with everything unbounded coming from outside? Here it is.
The guide to the project's lab of experiments says: “One frame is one evaluation of a fixed-depth circuit”. The host turns the crank. It never stops early.
Every weight so far was written by hand. The README's first funny use-case:
“unfreezing the weights and train them (what does that even do? Let's find out!)”
Take one gated product: a valve. Along its channel flows an input, three, times a weight, w. The opening is g plus b, never below nought.
With w a half, g a quarter, b minus a tenth: it opens nought point one five, and out comes nought point two two five.
Learning needs each number's slope, or gradient: nudge it, and how far does the output move?
Backwards, w's slope is three times the opening: nought point four five. g's is the channel itself: one and a half.
Lower b to minus four tenths. The valve shuts, and every slope behind it goes dark.
A README in the project warns: “Without any decay, a unit whose gate has closed gets no gradient and stays shut”.
The neurons of 1943 couldn't learn. These can, if you let them.
Almost every operation runs backwards by a rule like that: on the real arithmetic, not the rounding.
The README calls it fully differentiable: a slope everywhere. The project itself has doubts.
Ask the ramps which way to nudge the input. At almost every whole number: nowhere.
Differentiable as real arithmetic. But a decision has no slope to follow.
Only one demo learns: the learned gallery. From random weights, it learns to place the photos on rectangles you sketch.
Before each step, plain JavaScript pairs each photo with a rectangle. The network learns where. JavaScript decides who.
Each photo's edges pull toward its rectangle, but every pull is capped.
Far-off photos vote. They don't shout.
Six hundred steps a second, through the program's own backward pass.
An early fix snapped the sketch to a grid, in ordinary code. Cheng turned it down: “the spirit of the gallery is to learn something.”
To be fair, that's a small generic network, not a hand-written program unfrozen.
The lab did unfreeze one app's five design numbers to follow a drag. One gradient step solved nearly two in three moving frames.
A frozen program trained end to end inside a text-writing network, like nanoGPT? Not attempted. It hangs as a question.
Six commits in July. In August, none.
The record doesn't say why. So we won't guess.
July’s lab briefs listed established conclusions, to take as given. One: compiling ordinary code was a dead end.
Who tied it on? A conversation whose people go unnamed.
On the third of September, an AI agent’s review retired ten earlier claims, that one among them. Its narrower replacement: a defined numeric subset can be compiled.
It held about eight weeks.
One test, learning two additions, scored nought out of twenty. Multiply its error by a million, which should change nothing: twenty out of twenty. A tiny safety constant was swamping the slopes.
In July, a checker for the lab's compiler reported zero mismatches. The compiled code skipped an early return, and so did the checker.
As the docs warn, “That the two evaluators agree doesn't show that a program does what the JavaScript it replaces did.”
Every commit is Cheng Lou’s; most also credit a coding agent, Claude Code.
The review also names an earlier OpenAI agent, Codex. This film was written with Claude.
Mistakes and catches alike came from one process, under his direction.
In mid-September, he settled three questions.
Then October: six hundred and eighty-nine commits.
Nearly all of them in four days.
Cheng asked whether search on the GPU was “clearly more performant”, and if so, worth a demo.
A hundred thousand JSON documents, small text records, one per GPU lane, all running one small step.
So what is a GPU for? The demo's answer: “It is for many documents”.
On the thirteenth, a hedged write-up tied on a tag: the GPU is faster.
Search patterns are what Kleene, back in 1951, called regular events.
As the code says, a new pattern “writes cells and changes no program.”
A program can't go back, so search walks each document twice.
From the end, then the start: a longest match is only known after reading past its end.
The browser's pattern-matcher, RegExp, on one core: eight to twenty-eight milliseconds a keystroke. The search: eleven to fifteen.
One pattern makes it try every way back: over two seconds. The program never goes back: eleven milliseconds.
The same day, a review found RegExp had one of eighteen cores.
With eight workers, RegExp keeps up, and wins after a pause, except on that one pattern.
That tag held for hours.
The lab, with good grace: “RegExp is fast.”
On the fourteenth, Cheng gave the go-ahead: “Do it quick plz, then publish.”
That evening it went public: “My dear friends, I’d like to show you my latest toy project”.
On Hacker News, one commenter said it’s really “write your logic in a DSL that creates a neural-net-shaped circuit”. A DSL: a little language for one job.
Another saw a compiler. The docs side with the first: no tool converts your code.
Nine days after launch, a stranger tried four and a half: “you get 11.”
Turn our whole-number tag over: the landing page's hidden comment already said so. A promise that states its limits is kept.
Another asked what the website never said: “why?”
That's our blank tag. We'll keep it for the end.
About the lab, we found no public word: the strangers' pencils were gentler than its own.
One last experiment. The search demo's JSON highlighter stops at the first mistake.
Its parser is a table, and valid input never reads most of it.
Train only the unread entries, to keep going after a mistake, and valid JSON parses exactly as before.
Before testing, the lab tied on a tag: training can fill those entries. Then it fixed its rule for failure, and committed the test sets first.
JSON: “a clear success.”
Though on new kinds of mistake, and on whole payloads written by agents, hand-written rules still won.
For TOML, another format: “By the rule fixed beforehand the track failed”.
It lost to a one-line hand-written fallback, every run.
The README is careful: the failure “does not say that training cannot work there.”
This is how a belief should end: by a rule written before the test.
The third parser's final test hasn't run yet. That question stays open.
So does the lab's own list.
It says plainly: “a general JavaScript compiler” is “not delivered by these experiments.”
Every belief in the film hangs over the time it held.
Now re-hang them the way the loom does: each belief one layer after those it needs.
The film's teaching order, not history.
Send one wave of light through it. Every tag lights.
The struck ones ran too. Multiplied by nought.
Three beliefs are still argued over. Learn the weights, don't write them. Fully differentiable. And the README's claim to take “regular JavaScript”.
To the stranger's “why?”, the README's nearest answers: “for fun”, and “Let's find out!”
The notes window ends: “Wire one more neuron by hand”.
Who ties the next one on? Who doubts it? How long will it hold?
It's waiting for the next pair of hands.
